## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Statistical Learning for Scientific Imaging and Physical Measurements: Geosciences
  Official title       Apprentissage statistique pour l’imagerie scientifique et les mesures physiques : applications aux géosciences
  Instructors          J. KHERROUBI ; A. JAN (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 30 h (lectures 12 h, labs 18 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label}[Track I&I]{.badge .track}
  Language             French or English, materials in English (master-mva.com); French (Université Paris-Saclay)
  Assessment           “Évaluation continue non intégrale” (partial continuous assessment, Paris-Saclay); no weights shown
  Prerequisites        Linear algebra, probability and statistics, optimisation, Python programming (both official pages)
  Note on sources      master-mva.com lists the course in semester 1; the Université Paris-Saclay table places it in semester 2
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: students with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who want to learn how statistical learning is adapted to images and signals produced by physical sensors, with subsurface exploration and energy as the running case.

**Empirical first**: on synthetic well logs built to mimic real ones, a random forest reaches 97 % accuracy under random cross-validation and 49 % on wells it has never seen (code 7.3). Neither the model nor the data are at fault; the evaluation is. This course is about such traps, and about the physics that explains them.

Geophysical tools never photograph the rock. They send a seismic, electromagnetic, ultrasonic or mechanical field into the ground, record a response, and leave the rest to inference. The course follows that chain from acquisition to interpretation: describe the measurement, compress it, sharpen it, judge its quality, align it, enhance and repair it, classify and segment it, and finally invert it.

At each step it puts a classical method, a statistical-learning method and a deep-learning method side by side, and it asks what changes when the model leaves the laboratory. Closely related MVA courses are [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Image Denoising](../s1-image-denoising/index.html), [Sub-Pixel Image Processing](../s1-sub-pixel-image-processing/index.html) and [Machine Learning for Time Series](../s1-time-series/index.html); in semester 2, [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) and [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html) take several threads further.

### What you will be able to do

-   Write the forward model of a measurement system (well log, borehole image, seismic trace, ultrasonic echo) and read its resolution limits.
-   Compress images and logs with transform coding, PCA and learned codecs, and predict the distortion from the rate.
-   Formulate super-resolution as an ill-posed estimation problem and explain why mean-squared-error networks blur.
-   Choose and compute quality measures (PSNR, SSIM, noise estimates) and ranking metrics, and fit scores from pairwise expert preferences.
-   Align logs and images with cross-correlation, phase correlation, dynamic time warping and Procrustes registration.
-   Enhance contrast with histogram methods and fill gaps by variational and learned inpainting.
-   Train and validate facies classifiers and segmentation networks without leaking information across wells.
-   Solve linear and sparse inverse problems (Tikhonov, ISTA) and combine them with learning and physical constraints.
-   Diagnose distribution shift, quantify uncertainty with conformal prediction, and fit a model to compute and memory budgets.
-   Plan the path from a research prototype to a tool that interpreters can trust.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com presents modern statistical-learning and deep-learning methods for scientific imaging and for data from physical sensors. Its problems (image reconstruction, super-resolution, data alignment, contrast enhancement, segmentation, inverse problems) are shared by medical imaging, space, industrial vision, robotics and the geosciences.

Through real applications from subsurface exploration and the energy sector, it shows how to adapt AI methods to complex data acquired by advanced measurement systems. These data are images or signals and rest on several physics: electromagnetic, ultrasonic, mechanical and seismic.

The description stresses the challenges met by AI engineers in industry: limited or imperfectly annotated data, distribution shifts between environments, compute and memory constraints, and the need for robustness, interpretability and integration with physical models. It also covers the practices that turn a research prototype into a solution deployable at scale, presented as a concrete introduction to the job of AI engineer.

The content covers the whole processing chain, from data acquisition to interpretation, and combines theoretical foundations with industrial case studies. Several data sets and applications are announced in geology, corrosion and geo-energy.

The Université Paris-Saclay course detail ("Introduction à l'apprentissage statistique pour les géosciences") describes an introduction to statistical learning for the geosciences with applications in energy. Geophysical measurements are acquired with high-technology sensors in extreme conditions; they describe the subsurface to support critical decisions, and their several physics give interpreters complementary information.

It announces theoretical and practical content on traditional methods, conventional statistical-learning methods and deep-learning methods, and lists the module in the I&I track. Its learning objectives repeat the six themes of master-mva.com, which the table below matches to this page.

### Course outline

-   **Review: linear algebra, signals, probability and optimisation** — the SVD, convolution and sampling, MAP estimation, gradient descent and convolutional layers.
-   **Measurement systems: images and logs** — forward models of well logs, borehole images, seismic traces and ultrasonic echoes.
-   **Compression** — transform coding, PCA, quantisation and the rate–distortion limit, then learned codecs.
-   **Super-resolution** — why the problem is ill-posed, what a trained network estimates, and how deep networks are built for it.
-   **Quality measures and ranking** — full-reference and no-reference quality, ranking metrics and learning to rank.
-   **Data alignment** — shifts, warps and rotations between logs, images and seismic.
-   **Contrast enhancement and inpainting** — histogram methods and the filling of gaps.
-   **Classification and segmentation** — facies from logs, features in images, and honest validation.
-   **Inversion** — from measurements back to rock properties, with regularisation, sparsity, physics and learning.
-   **From prototype to deployment: the industrial challenges** — imperfect labels, distribution shift, uncertainty, budgets and deployment.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — self-study on current research.

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session, even quickly: the SVD, the convolution theorem and the MAP formula come back in almost every chapter.
-   After each session, run the chapter's code block, change one parameter, and predict the result before looking.
-   Do the exercises listed in the session plan in the same week; the ★ ones check the session, the ★★ ones prepare the exam.
-   Keep one notebook per chapter with a common data generator (synthetic logs and borehole images): the labs reuse it.
-   The environment is Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch on CPU; every code block runs in less than about 30 s on a laptop.
-   Start the project (see [Projects and assessment](#projects)) at the kick-off of session 10, once classification (session 8) and inversion (session 9) have been seen.

## 0. Review: linear algebra, signals, probability and optimisation {#ch0}

Every method of this course is a variation on one situation: an unknown property, a measurement, and an operator that links them. This review gathers the M1 tools that the later chapters use without stopping: the singular value decomposition, convolution and sampling, the Bayesian reading of regularisation, gradient descent, and the convolutional layer.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Singular value decomposition and pseudo-inverse]{.tag} Every matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ of rank $r$ factorises as
$$
A = U \Sigma V^\top = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i\, u_i v_i^\top, \qquad \sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_r > 0,
$$
with orthonormal families $(u_i)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $(v_i)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$. The **pseudo-inverse** is
$$
A^+ = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \frac{1}{\sigma_i}\, v_i u_i^\top .
$$
The vector $x^+ = A^+ y$ minimises $\|Ax - y\|_2$, and among all minimisers it has the smallest norm.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — Eckart–Young]{.tag} For $k < r$, let $A_k = \sum_{i \le k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top$. For every matrix $B$ of rank at most $k$:
$$
\|A - B\|_F^2 \;\ge\; \|A - A_k\|_F^2 = \sum_{i > k} \sigma_i^2 .
$$

::: proof
Weyl's inequality for singular values states that $\sigma_{i+j-1}(X + Y) \le \sigma_i(X) + \sigma_j(Y)$.

Apply it with $X = A - B$, $Y = B$ and $j = k + 1$. Since $\operatorname{rank} B \le k$, $\sigma_{k+1}(B) = 0$, hence for every $i$:
$$
\sigma_{i+k}(A) \le \sigma_i(A - B).
$$

Summing the squares gives
$$
\|A - B\|_F^2 = \sum_i \sigma_i(A - B)^2 \ge \sum_i \sigma_{i+k}(A)^2 = \sum_{i > k} \sigma_i^2 .
$$
For $B = A_k$ the residual is $\sum_{i > k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top$, whose squared Frobenius norm is exactly that sum, by orthonormality. [∎]{.qed}
:::

This is the theorem behind PCA compression (ch. 2) and behind every truncated-SVD estimator of ch. 8.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Circular convolution and discrete Fourier transform]{.tag} For $x, h \in \mathbb{C}^n$ with indices taken modulo $n$:
$$
(x \circledast h)_k = \sum_{m=0}^{n-1} x_m\, h_{k-m}, \qquad \hat x_\ell = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} x_k\, e^{-2i\pi k\ell/n}.
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Convolution theorem]{.tag} The DFT turns convolution into a pointwise product:
$$
\widehat{x \circledast h}_\ell = \hat x_\ell\, \hat h_\ell .
$$

::: proof
Substitute the definition and set $j = k - m$ (modulo $n$):
$$
\sum_k \sum_m x_m h_{k-m} e^{-2i\pi k\ell/n} = \sum_m x_m e^{-2i\pi m\ell/n} \sum_j h_j e^{-2i\pi j\ell/n} = \hat x_\ell\, \hat h_\ell .
$$
The exchange of sums is legitimate because both are finite. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Consequences used later: a linear, shift-invariant tool acts frequency by frequency; deconvolution divides by $\hat h_\ell$ and explodes where it is small (ch. 8); cross-correlations for all shifts cost $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ with the FFT (ch. 5).
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Sampling (Shannon–Nyquist) and aliasing]{.tag} Let $x(t)$ have finite energy and a Fourier transform supported in $[-B, B]$. If the sampling rate satisfies $f_s > 2B$, the samples determine the signal:
$$
x(t) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} x\!\left(\tfrac{k}{f_s}\right) \operatorname{sinc}(f_s t - k), \qquad \operatorname{sinc}(u) = \frac{\sin \pi u}{\pi u}.
$$
If instead $f_s < 2B$, a cosine of frequency $f$ and one of frequency $|f - m f_s|$, for an integer $m$, take the same values on the grid (aliasing).

::: proof
*Sketch.* By the Poisson summation formula, the spectrum of the sampled signal is the periodisation of $\hat x$ with period $f_s$. The copies do not overlap when $f_s > 2B$, so an ideal low-pass filter on $[-f_s/2, f_s/2]$ recovers $\hat x$; in time, that filter is the sinc interpolation.

For aliasing, the two arguments below differ by $2\pi m k$, so for every integer $k$:
$$
\cos(2\pi f k / f_s) = \cos(2\pi (f - m f_s) k / f_s). \qquad
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Every tool samples, in depth or in time. The sampling interval fixes the highest frequency that can be recovered; super-resolution (ch. 3) is precisely about what lies beyond it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — MAP estimation is regularised least squares]{.tag} Let $y = Ax + \varepsilon$ with noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$ and prior $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2 I)$. The posterior mode is

::: key
[Key result — the regularised least-squares estimator]{.tag}
$$
\hat x_\lambda = \arg\min_x \|y - Ax\|_2^2 + \lambda \|x\|_2^2 = (A^\top A + \lambda I)^{-1} A^\top y, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}.
$$
:::

::: proof
Up to a constant, the negative log-posterior is
$$
\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y - Ax\|^2 + \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|x\|^2 .
$$
Multiply by $2\sigma^2$. The result is a strictly convex quadratic, since its Hessian $2(A^\top A + \lambda I)$ is positive definite. Its unique minimiser cancels the gradient $2A^\top(Ax - y) + 2\lambda x$, which gives the formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The ratio of noise variance to prior variance is the regularisation weight: the less we trust the data, the more we lean on the prior. Chapters 3 and 8 use this estimator.
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.7 — Gradient descent on a smooth convex function]{.tag} Let $f$ be convex with an $L$-Lipschitz gradient and a minimiser $x^\star$. The iterates $x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{1}{L} \nabla f(x_k)$ satisfy
$$
f(x_k) - f(x^\star) \le \frac{L\, \|x_0 - x^\star\|^2}{2k}.
$$

::: proof
*Sketch.* The descent lemma gives
$$
f(x_{k+1}) \le f(x_k) - \frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 .
$$
Combined with convexity, this yields
$$
f(x_{k+1}) - f^\star \le \frac{L}{2}\left(\|x_k - x^\star\|^2 - \|x_{k+1} - x^\star\|^2\right).
$$
Summing over $k$ telescopes the right-hand side, and the values decrease, so the last one is below the average. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The same argument proves the convergence of ISTA in ch. 8.
::::

:::: def
[Definition 0.8 — Convolutional layer and receptive field]{.tag} A one-dimensional convolutional layer with kernel size $k$ maps $C$ input channels to $C'$ output channels:
$$
y_{c,t} = b_c + \sum_{c'=1}^{C} \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} W_{c,c',j}\, x_{c',\, t + j - \lfloor k/2 \rfloor},
$$
followed by a pointwise nonlinearity such as $\mathrm{ReLU}(u) = \max(u, 0)$. It commutes with translations, and its weights are shared across positions.

Stacking $L$ such layers with stride 1 gives each output a **receptive field** of $1 + L(k - 1)$ input samples. The proof is an induction: each layer widens the field by $k - 1$ samples ($\lfloor k/2 \rfloor$ on each side when $k$ is odd).
::::

Two-dimensional layers work the same way on images. Encoder–decoder networks with skip connections (U-Net, ch. 7.2) combine a large receptive field with precise localisation.

**Code 0.9 — checking the convolution theorem, aliasing and least squares.**

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 64
x, h = rng.standard_normal(n), rng.standard_normal(n)

# circular convolution, directly and through the DFT (Proposition 0.4)
direct = np.array([sum(x[m] * h[(k - m) % n] for m in range(n)) for k in range(n)])
via_fft = np.real(np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(x) * np.fft.fft(h)))
print("max |direct - FFT| =", np.abs(direct - via_fft).max())

# aliasing (Theorem 0.5): 70 Hz sampled at 100 Hz looks like 30 Hz
t = np.arange(50) / 100.0
gap = np.abs(np.cos(2 * np.pi * 70 * t) - np.cos(2 * np.pi * 30 * t)).max()
print("max |cos(70 Hz) - cos(30 Hz)| on the grid =", gap)

# least squares through the pseudo-inverse (Definition 0.1)
A = rng.standard_normal((20, 5))
y = rng.standard_normal(20)
x_ls = np.linalg.pinv(A) @ y
print("normal equations residual:", np.abs(A.T @ (A @ x_ls - y)).max())
```

All three printed numbers are at the level of rounding errors (about $10^{-14}$): the two convolutions agree, the 70 Hz and 30 Hz cosines coincide on a 100 Hz grid, and the pseudo-inverse solves the normal equations.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 0
:::

-   The SVD diagonalises any linear operator; truncating it gives the best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young).
-   Convolution becomes multiplication in the Fourier domain, and sampling fixes the highest recoverable frequency.
-   A Gaussian prior turns least squares into ridge regression, with weight equal to the ratio of noise to prior variance.
-   Gradient descent on a smooth convex function converges at rate $1/k$.
-   A stack of convolutional layers has a receptive field that grows linearly with depth.
::::

## 1. Measurement systems: images and logs {#ch1}

A geoscientist never observes porosity, a fluid or a fault directly. A tool emits a physical field, records a response, and the property is inferred. This chapter models that chain, so that every later task (compressing, enhancing, aligning, classifying, inverting) is stated on the right object.

### 1.1 Measurement as a forward model

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Measurement system]{.tag} A measurement system links an unknown property field $x$ (for instance resistivity as a function of position) to recorded data $y$ through
$$
y = \mathcal{M}(x) + \varepsilon .
$$
The **forward operator** $\mathcal{M}$ contains the physics of the probing field, the response of the tool and the sampling; $\varepsilon$ is the noise.

Three numbers summarise a tool: its **resolution** (the smallest feature it separates), its **depth of investigation** (how far from the sensor it sees) and its **sampling interval**.
:::

Computing $y$ from $x$ is the forward problem, a simulation that is usually well-posed. Recovering $x$ from $y$ is the inverse problem of ch. 8. Most "images" of this course are not photographs: each pixel is a physical measurement with a unit, a resolution and an error.

| Physics | What the tool measures | Typical data | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seismic (elastic waves from surface sources) | reflected amplitudes and travel times | 2D sections, 3D cubes | structure, faults, facies, impedance |
| Electromagnetic (galvanic or induction) | electrical resistivity or conductivity | logs; resistivity borehole images | fluids (Archie's law), bedding, fractures |
| Ultrasonic (pulse–echo) | echo amplitude and travel time | borehole and casing images | borehole shape, breakouts, casing thickness and corrosion |
| Mechanical (sonic waves, calipers) | wave slowness; borehole diameter | logs, full waveforms | elastic moduli, porosity, borehole condition |
| Nuclear (often run together) | natural gamma rays, density, neutron response | logs | clay content, porosity |

### 1.2 Well logs

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Well log]{.tag} A well log is a depth-indexed multivariate series
$$
x(z_k) \in \mathbb{R}^p, \qquad z_k = z_0 + k\, \Delta z, \quad k = 0, \dots, n - 1,
$$
whose $p$ curves (gamma ray, resistivity, density, neutron, sonic…) are recorded by tools pulled along the borehole. Conventional logs are sampled every few tens of centimetres or less; each curve has its own unit, range and missing intervals.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — The vertical response of a tool is a convolution]{.tag} Let a tool average the true property with a vertical response $g \ge 0$ of integral 1:
$$
m(z) = \int g(z - z')\, x(z')\, dz' .
$$
If $g$ is a box of width $w$, a bed of thickness $h < w$ with contrast $\Delta$ over a uniform background appears with an apparent contrast whose absolute value is at most
$$
\frac{h}{w}\, |\Delta| .
$$

::: proof
Write $x = x_0 + \Delta\, \mathbb{1}_{\text{bed}}$. Then
$$
m(z) - x_0 = \Delta \cdot \frac{|\text{window}(z) \cap \text{bed}|}{w}.
$$
The intersection of a window of length $w$ with a bed of length $h < w$ has length at most $h$, and exactly $h$ when the window covers the bed. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — A thin sand in a shale]{.tag} A tool with a 60 cm box response logs a 15 cm sand (gamma ray 30 API) inside a shale (110 API), so $\Delta = -80$ API. In absolute value, the apparent contrast is at most
$$
\frac{15}{60} \times 80 = 20 \text{ API},
$$
so the log reads about 90 API at best at the sand and the sand is almost invisible. Thinly laminated reservoirs are underestimated for this reason, and the Fourier view (Proposition 0.4) says why: the tool is a low-pass filter.
:::

::: note
[Physics as a model — Archie's law]{.tag} Archie (1942) observed that, in clean formations, the true resistivity $R_t$ relates to porosity $\phi$ and water saturation $S_w$ through
$$
R_t = \frac{a\, R_w}{\phi^{m} S_w^{n}},
$$
with $R_w$ the water resistivity and empirical constants $a$, $m$, $n$. Resistivity spans several orders of magnitude, so models work with $\log R_t$; in that variable Archie's law is linear. Such laws are the "physical models" with which learned models must stay consistent (ch. 8, ch. 9).
:::

::: note
[Physics as a model — the sonic log]{.tag} A sonic tool times a compressional wave refracted along the borehole wall and logs its slowness $\Delta t = 1/v$, in µs/ft. In a clean, consolidated rock, Wyllie, Gregory and Gardner (1956) add the travel times through the pore fluid and the matrix:
$$
\Delta t = \phi\, \Delta t_f + (1 - \phi)\, \Delta t_m, \qquad \phi = \frac{\Delta t - \Delta t_m}{\Delta t_f - \Delta t_m}.
$$
With a sandstone matrix at 55.5 µs/ft and water at 189 µs/ft, a reading of 80 µs/ft gives $\phi = 24.5 / 133.5 \approx 18$ %. A mechanical caliper logs the borehole diameter; enlarged intervals flag pad readings as unreliable (ch. 4.2).
:::

### 1.3 Borehole images

An imaging tool records many logs around the borehole wall at once. Resistivity tools press several pads against the wall and cover part of the circumference; rotating ultrasonic transducers cover all of it. Unrolling the cylinder gives an image $I(z, \varphi)$, with depth $z$ downwards and azimuth $\varphi \in [0, 2\pi)$ across.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — A plane cuts the borehole along a sinusoid]{.tag} Let a vertical cylindrical borehole of radius $r$ be cut by a plane of dip $\theta$ (angle to the horizontal) that dips towards azimuth $\varphi_d$. In the unrolled image, the trace of the plane is
$$
z(\varphi) = z_0 + r \tan\theta \, \cos(\varphi - \varphi_d).
$$

::: proof
Take the borehole axis as the $z$ axis. Depth along the plane increases with slope $\tan\theta$ in the direction $(\cos\varphi_d, \sin\varphi_d)$, so the plane is
$$
z = z_0 + \tan\theta\,(X \cos\varphi_d + Y \sin\varphi_d).
$$
A point of the wall at azimuth $\varphi$ has $X = r\cos\varphi$ and $Y = r\sin\varphi$. Substituting and using the identity
$$
\cos\varphi\cos\varphi_d + \sin\varphi\sin\varphi_d = \cos(\varphi - \varphi_d)
$$
gives the formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Fitting is linear.** Expanding the cosine, $z(\varphi) = a + b\cos\varphi + c\sin\varphi$ with $b = r\tan\theta\cos\varphi_d$ and $c = r\tan\theta\sin\varphi_d$. Least squares on picked points gives $(a, b, c)$, then
$$
\tan\theta = \frac{\sqrt{b^2 + c^2}}{r}, \qquad \varphi_d = \operatorname{atan2}(c, b).
$$
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.6 — Sizes of sinusoids]{.tag} In an 8.5-inch borehole, $r = 10.8$ cm.

-   A bed dipping at 30° gives an amplitude $r \tan 30° = 6.2$ cm, so the sinusoid spans 12.5 cm from top to bottom.
-   A fracture dipping at 80° gives $r \tan 80° = 61$ cm: its sinusoid spans 1.22 m.

Steep fractures therefore cross many image rows, and a pad gap (ch. 6.2) cuts them into separate pieces.
:::

### 1.4 Seismic data: the convolutional model

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Impedance, reflectivity and the convolutional trace]{.tag} The **acoustic impedance** of a layer is $Z = \rho v$ (density times velocity). At normal incidence, the interface between layers 1 and 2 reflects a fraction
$$
R = \frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}
$$
of the amplitude; the formula follows from the continuity of pressure and particle velocity at the interface (Sheriff and Geldart, 1995).

The **convolutional model** writes a trace as
$$
s(t) = (w * r)(t) + n(t), \qquad r(t) = \sum_k R_k\, \delta(t - t_k),
$$
where $t_k$ is the two-way travel time to interface $k$ and $w$ is the source wavelet, often a Ricker wavelet
$$
w(t) = (1 - 2\pi^2 f^2 t^2)\, e^{-\pi^2 f^2 t^2}.
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — Thin beds and tuning]{.tag} A bed with top reflection $R$ and base reflection $-R$, separated by a two-way time $\tau$, produces
$$
s(t) = R\,[w(t) - w(t - \tau)] = R\, \tau\, w'(t) + \mathcal{O}(\tau^2).
$$
Below the resolution limit, the amplitude grows linearly with the thickness and the shape is the derivative of the wavelet; near a quarter wavelength the two reflections interfere constructively (tuning).

::: proof
Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives $w(t - \tau) = w(t) - \tau w'(t) + \mathcal{O}(\tau^2)$, uniformly in $t$ since $w''$ is bounded. Substitute into $R[w(t) - w(t - \tau)]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.9 — Tuning with numbers]{.tag} Take $v = 3000$ m/s and a 30 Hz Ricker wavelet, so the wavelength is $\lambda = v / f = 100$ m. The bed has $Z_2 = 7.5 \times 10^6$ in a background $Z_1 = 6.0 \times 10^6$ (SI units), so $R = 0.111$.

Code 1.11 gives the peak amplitude of the trace as a function of the thickness $h$:

| $h$ (m) | 5 | 10 | 20 | 25 | 40 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| peak amplitude | 0.060 | 0.123 | 0.161 | 0.149 | 0.113 | 0.111 |

Below 10 m the amplitude is roughly proportional to $h$ (Proposition 1.8). It peaks near 20 m, 45 % above a single reflection, close to the classical $\lambda/4 = 25$ m (Widess, 1973). From 60 m on, the two reflections are separate.
:::

The scale gap is the central fact of subsurface data. Seismic resolves tens of metres over kilometres; logs resolve decimetres along one well; borehole images resolve centimetres around it. Tying these scales together is the job of alignment (ch. 5) and inversion (ch. 8).

### 1.5 Ultrasonic pulse–echo and casing corrosion

An ultrasonic transducer emits a short pulse and records the echo. The travel time $t$ to a reflector at distance $d$ in a fluid of sound speed $c$ gives $d = ct/2$; rotating the transducer maps the borehole radius around the wall, which reveals ovalisation and breakouts.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.10 — Thickness resonance of a plate]{.tag} A pulse entering a steel plate (a casing) of thickness $e$ reverberates between its two faces. With compressional speed $c$ in the plate, the echo train resonates at
$$
f_n = \frac{n\, c}{2e}, \qquad n = 1, 2, \dots
$$

::: proof
Inside the plate, the wave is reflected at both faces by a fluid of lower impedance, so each reflection flips the sign and a round trip adds no net sign change. Successive echoes are then delayed by a path of $2e$, and they add in phase when $2e$ is a whole number $n$ of wavelengths $c / f$, which is the stated condition. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $c \approx 5900$ m/s in steel and $e = 10$ mm, $f_1 \approx 295$ kHz. Corrosion thins the casing, so the resonance frequency rises; measured around and along the well, it becomes a thickness image $e(z, \varphi)$ on which metal loss is segmented (ch. 7.2).

Electromagnetic inspection rests on another physics: eddy currents induced in the metal decay over the skin depth
$$
\delta = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\omega \mu \sigma}},
$$
which depends on the frequency $\omega$, the magnetic permeability $\mu$ and the conductivity $\sigma$. Lower frequencies probe deeper.

### 1.6 What makes these data hard

-   **Physical units and dynamic range.** Resistivity spans orders of magnitude, so it is modelled in $\log$ scale; each curve has its own noise and artefacts.
-   **Several scales.** Each tool sees its own resolution and depth of investigation (Example 1.9).
-   **Labels are interpretations.** Facies, faults or fractures are drawn by experts who may disagree, and labelled wells are few (ch. 9.1).
-   **Every well is a new environment.** Tool generation, borehole size, drilling mud and geology change the input distribution (ch. 7.1, ch. 9.2).
-   **Volumes and budgets.** 3D surveys are large and downhole links are slow (ch. 2, ch. 9.4).
-   **Costly decisions.** Predictions feed drilling and production decisions, so uncertainty and interpretability matter (ch. 9.3).

**Code 1.11 — a synthetic seismogram, tuning, and a sinusoid fit.**

```python
import numpy as np

# Ricker wavelet, 30 Hz peak frequency, 1 ms sampling
dt, f = 0.001, 30.0
t = np.arange(-0.1, 0.1 + dt, dt)
w = (1 - 2 * (np.pi * f * t) ** 2) * np.exp(-(np.pi * f * t) ** 2)

# a bed of impedance Z2 inside a background Z1, velocity 3000 m/s
v, Z1, Z2 = 3000.0, 6.0e6, 7.5e6
R = (Z2 - Z1) / (Z2 + Z1)                  # Definition 1.7
print(f"R = {R:.4f}")
for h in [5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 60]:  # thickness in metres
    r = np.zeros(1000)
    k = int(round(2 * h / v / dt))         # two-way time in samples
    r[400], r[400 + k] = R, -R             # top and base reflections
    s = np.convolve(r, w, mode="same")     # convolutional model
    print(f"h = {h:2d} m   peak amplitude = {np.abs(s).max():.4f}")

# Theorem 1.5: fit a sinusoid to noisy picks on a borehole image
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
radius = 0.108                              # 8.5 in borehole, metres
dip, azi, z0 = np.deg2rad(30), np.deg2rad(120), 1500.0
phi = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, 40))
z = z0 + radius * np.tan(dip) * np.cos(phi - azi) + 0.003 * rng.standard_normal(40)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(phi), np.cos(phi), np.sin(phi)])
a, b, c = np.linalg.lstsq(X, z, rcond=None)[0]
print("dip  =", np.rad2deg(np.arctan(np.hypot(b, c) / radius)).round(2), "deg")
print("azimuth =", (np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(c, b)) % 360).round(1), "deg")
```

With 3 mm of picking noise on 40 points, the fit returns a dip of 30.06° and an azimuth of 120.0°, against 30° and 120° in truth.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::

-   Every data set is $y = \mathcal{M}(x) + \varepsilon$; resolution, depth of investigation and sampling describe $\mathcal{M}$.
-   A log is the true property convolved with the tool response: thin beds lose contrast in proportion $h / w$.
-   Planes appear as sinusoids on borehole images; dip and azimuth follow from a linear least-squares fit.
-   A seismic trace is reflectivity convolved with a wavelet; thin beds tune near a quarter wavelength.
-   Ultrasonic echoes give distances and, through plate resonance, casing thickness and corrosion.
::::

## 2. Compression {#ch2}

Subsurface data are large, and the channels that carry them can be tiny. A 3D seismic survey can reach terabytes; while drilling, data computed downhole travel to the surface by mud-pulse telemetry, at rates of the order of a few bits to a few tens of bits per second. This chapter asks how many bits a signal really needs for a given error.

### 2.1 Rate, distortion and quality

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Codec, rate, distortion, PSNR]{.tag} A **codec** is a pair of maps: an encoder from signals $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ to bit strings, and a decoder from bit strings back to reconstructions $\hat x$. Its **rate** $R$ is the expected number of bits per sample, its **distortion** the mean squared error
$$
D = \frac{1}{n}\, \mathbb{E}\, \|x - \hat x\|_2^2 .
$$
For images with peak value $P$ (1 for images in $[0, 1]$, 255 for 8-bit images), the **peak signal-to-noise ratio** is
$$
\mathrm{PSNR} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{P^2}{\mathrm{MSE}} \quad \text{(in dB)}.
$$
:::

PSNR is only a starting point: ch. 4 discusses measures that track structure and the downstream task.

### 2.2 Transform coding

The classical recipe has three steps: transform the signal into coefficients that concentrate its energy, quantise the coefficients, and code the quantised values without loss (entropy coding).

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Orthonormal transforms preserve the error]{.tag} If $T$ is orthonormal ($T^\top T = I$) and $c = Tx$, $\hat c$ are coefficients, then
$$
\|x - T^\top \hat c\|_2 = \|c - \hat c\|_2 .
$$

::: proof
A square orthonormal matrix also satisfies $T T^\top = I$, hence
$$
\|T^\top (c - \hat c)\|_2^2 = (c - \hat c)^\top T T^\top (c - \hat c) = \|c - \hat c\|_2^2 . \qquad
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

The error can therefore be budgeted coefficient by coefficient.
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Best $k$-term approximation]{.tag} In an orthonormal basis, among all approximations that keep $k$ coefficients of $x$ and set the others to zero, the smallest error is obtained by keeping the $k$ coefficients of largest magnitude. The squared error is the sum of the squares of the discarded coefficients.

::: proof
By Proposition 2.2, keeping a set $S$ of $k$ coefficients leaves the error $\sum_{i \notin S} c_i^2$. This sum is smallest when the complement of $S$ holds the $n - k$ smallest values of $c_i^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — PCA is the optimal linear code]{.tag} Let $x$ be a zero-mean random vector with covariance $C = \sum_{i} \lambda_i e_i e_i^\top$, where $\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n$. For every orthogonal projector $P$ of rank $k$:
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|x - Px\|^2 \;\ge\; \sum_{i > k} \lambda_i ,
$$
with equality when $P$ projects onto $\mathrm{span}(e_1, \dots, e_k)$.

::: proof
1.  Write $P = Q Q^\top$ with $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ orthonormal. Since $I - P$ is a projector,
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\|x - Px\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\, x^\top (I - P) x = \operatorname{tr}(C) - \operatorname{tr}(Q^\top C Q).
    $$
2.  Expand in the eigenbasis:
    $$
    \operatorname{tr}(Q^\top C Q) = \sum_i \lambda_i\, \|Q^\top e_i\|^2 .
    $$
    The weights $\|Q^\top e_i\|^2$ lie in $[0, 1]$ and sum to $\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top Q) = k$.
3.  A weighted sum of the $\lambda_i$ with such weights is at most $\lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_k$: move weight towards the largest values. Equality holds for $Q = [e_1, \dots, e_k]$.
4.  Hence
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\|x - Px\|^2 \ge \operatorname{tr}(C) - \sum_{i \le k} \lambda_i = \sum_{i > k} \lambda_i . \qquad
    $$
    [∎]{.qed}
:::

On data, $C$ is the empirical covariance and Theorem 0.2 gives the same subspace through the SVD of the centred data matrix.
::::

PCA must transmit its basis, which is costly. The discrete cosine transform (DCT) needs none, and for strongly correlated stationary signals it is close to the PCA basis (Ahmed, Natarajan and Rao, 1974); this is why JPEG uses it. Wavelets (Mallat, 2009) suit piecewise-smooth signals, such as blocky logs, because only coefficients near the jumps are large.

### 2.3 Quantisation and the rate–distortion limit

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Error of a uniform quantiser]{.tag} Rounding to the nearest multiple of a step $\Delta$ makes an error $e \in [-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]$. If the signal varies on a scale much larger than $\Delta$, the error is close to uniform on that interval, and
$$
\mathbb{E}\, e^2 \approx \frac{\Delta^2}{12} .
$$

::: proof
For $e$ uniform on $[-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\, e^2 = \frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} u^2\, du = \frac{\Delta^2}{12}.
$$
The uniformity is the high-resolution approximation: a smooth density is almost constant over each cell. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.6 — Rate–distortion function of a Gaussian source (Shannon)]{.tag} For independent samples of $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, the smallest rate at which a distortion $D \le \sigma^2$ can be reached is
$$
R(D) = \frac{1}{2} \log_2 \frac{\sigma^2}{D}.
$$

::: key
[Key result — six decibels per bit]{.tag}
$$
D(R) = \sigma^2\, 2^{-2R}: \quad \text{each extra bit per sample divides the distortion by 4, a gain of } 6.02 \text{ dB}.
$$
:::

::: proof
*Lower bound.* Any codec at rate $R$ satisfies $R \ge I(X; \hat X)$, the mutual information. Since the Gaussian has maximal entropy for a given variance,
$$
I(X; \hat X) = h(X) - h(X \mid \hat X) \ge h(X) - h(X - \hat X) \ge \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2(2\pi e \sigma^2) - \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2(2\pi e D).
$$
*Achievability* uses random coding over long blocks; see Cover and Thomas (2006, ch. 10). [∎]{.qed}
:::

For independent components $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_i^2)$, the optimal allocation is **reverse water-filling**: each component receives the distortion $D_i = \min(\theta, \sigma_i^2)$ for a common level $\theta$. Components with variance below $\theta$ are not coded at all, which is exactly why discarding small transform coefficients is sound.
::::

### 2.4 Learned compression

-   **Linear autoencoders.** A network $x \mapsto W_2 W_1 x$ trained with squared error learns the PCA subspace: all its local minima are global and span the top principal directions (Baldi and Hornik, 1989). Theorem 2.4 is therefore the baseline of every learned codec.
-   **Nonlinear transform coding.** An encoder $f_\theta$, a quantiser $Q$, an entropy model $p_\psi$ of the quantised code, and a decoder $g_\phi$ are trained together on a rate–distortion loss (Ballé, Laparra and Simoncelli, 2017).
-   **The training trick.** Rounding has zero gradient, so during training $Q$ is replaced by additive uniform noise on $[-1/2, 1/2]$, which has the same error statistics as Proposition 2.5.

The loss reads
$$
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}\big[-\log_2 p_\psi(Q(f_\theta(x)))\big] + \lambda\, \mathbb{E}\, \|x - g_\phi(Q(f_\theta(x)))\|^2 ,
$$
where the first term is the code length after entropy coding and $\lambda$ selects a point on the rate–distortion curve.

Industrial constraints shape the design. The encoder runs downhole on small, hot, low-power hardware, while the decoder runs at the surface and can be large (ch. 9.4). And a codec must not invent geology: a compressed image is judged on the features an interpreter picks from it (ch. 4.1), not only on its PSNR.

::: ex
[Example 2.7 — DCT against patch PCA on a borehole-like image]{.tag} Code 2.8 builds a 256 × 256 unrolled image with dipping beds, two fractures and noise, scaled to $[0, 1]$.

-   Keeping the largest 1 %, 5 % and 10 % of global DCT coefficients gives 28.7, 32.7 and 34.2 dB.
-   PCA on 8 × 8 patches with 3 or 6 components out of 64 (4.7 % and 9.4 %) gives 28.0 and 30.8 dB.
-   Measured quantisation errors match $\Delta^2 / 12$ within 2 % at 4, 6 and 8 bits.

The percentages ignore the cost of coding the positions of the kept DCT coefficients and the PCA basis; a real codec must pay for both.
:::

**Code 2.8 — transform coding of a synthetic borehole image.**

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import dctn, idctn

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
H, W = 256, 256
z, j = np.mgrid[0:H, 0:W].astype(float)                    # depth, azimuth index
phi = 2 * np.pi * j / W
# synthetic unrolled borehole image: dipping layers + two fractures + noise
img = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (z + 12 * np.cos(phi - 1.0)) / 23)
for z0, amp in [(80, 30), (170, 18)]:
    img += 2.0 * np.exp(-((z - z0 - amp * np.cos(phi - 2.5)) / 1.5) ** 2)
img += 0.1 * rng.standard_normal((H, W))
img = (img - img.min()) / (img.max() - img.min())          # range [0, 1]

def psnr(x, y, peak=1.0):                                  # Definition 2.1
    return 10 * np.log10(peak ** 2 / np.mean((x - y) ** 2))

c = dctn(img, norm="ortho")                                # orthonormal 2D DCT
for frac in [0.01, 0.05, 0.10]:
    thr = np.quantile(np.abs(c), 1 - frac)                 # keep the largest (Thm 2.3)
    rec = idctn(np.where(np.abs(c) >= thr, c, 0), norm="ortho")
    print(f"DCT, keep {frac:4.0%}: PSNR = {psnr(img, rec):5.2f} dB")

# PCA on 8x8 patches (Theorem 2.4): k of 64 coefficients per patch
P = img.reshape(32, 8, 32, 8).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(-1, 64)
mu = P.mean(0)
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(P - mu, full_matrices=False)
for k in [1, 3, 6]:
    rec = (P - mu) @ Vt[:k].T @ Vt[:k] + mu
    rec = rec.reshape(32, 32, 8, 8).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(H, W)
    print(f"PCA, k = {k} ({k / 64:4.1%}): PSNR = {psnr(img, rec):5.2f} dB")

# uniform quantisation (Proposition 2.5): measured vs predicted MSE
for bits in [4, 6, 8]:
    step = 1.0 / 2 ** bits
    q = (np.floor(img / step) + 0.5) * step
    print(f"{bits} bits: MSE = {np.mean((img - q) ** 2):.2e}, step^2/12 = {step ** 2 / 12:.2e}")
```

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::

-   Rate is bits per sample, distortion is mean squared error, PSNR is distortion on a log scale.
-   With an orthonormal transform, keeping the largest coefficients is optimal for a given number of terms.
-   PCA is the optimal linear code; the DCT approximates it without transmitting a basis.
-   A uniform quantiser costs $\Delta^2 / 12$; for a Gaussian source each bit buys about 6 dB.
-   Learned codecs train encoder, entropy model and decoder on a rate–distortion loss, with noise in place of rounding.
::::

## 3. Super-resolution {#ch3}

Logs are averaged over decimetres, seismic over tens of metres, and some imaging tools are coarser than the features interpreters need. Super-resolution estimates a finer signal from a coarser one. This chapter shows that the problem has infinitely many exact solutions, and that what a trained network returns depends on its loss.

### 3.1 The degradation model

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Degradation model]{.tag} A fine signal $x \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is observed through a blur $h$ (the tool response, Proposition 1.3), a decimation $S_s$ that keeps one sample in $s$, and noise:
$$
y = S_s(h * x) + n = A x + n, \qquad A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times N}, \quad m = N / s .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Super-resolution is not unique]{.tag} The kernel of $A$ has dimension at least $N - m = N(1 - 1/s)$. Every $x + v$ with $v \in \ker A$ produces the same noise-free data as $x$.

::: proof
By the rank–nullity theorem, $\dim \ker A = N - \operatorname{rank} A \ge N - m$. For $v \in \ker A$, $A(x + v) = Ax$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Super-resolution is therefore a choice inside an affine space of dimension at least $N(1 - 1/s)$, and only prior knowledge can make it. In Fourier terms (Theorem 0.5), frequencies above the coarse Nyquist limit are folded onto lower ones and cannot be told apart from them without a prior.

### 3.2 Classical estimators

-   **Interpolation** (nearest, linear, cubic, sinc) assumes the signal is smooth or band-limited; it never restores what the blur removed.
-   **Regularised inversion** chooses the smoothest consistent signal, with $D$ a finite-difference matrix:
    $$
    \hat x = \arg\min_x \|y - Ax\|^2 + \lambda \|Dx\|^2 = (A^\top A + \lambda D^\top D)^{-1} A^\top y .
    $$
    The matrix is invertible when $\ker A \cap \ker D = \{0\}$, since the quadratic form then vanishes only at zero.
-   **Example-based regression** learns the map from coarse to fine patches on pairs where both are known.

### 3.3 What a trained estimator converges to

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — The MMSE estimator is the posterior mean]{.tag} Let $\mathbb{E}\|X\|^2 < \infty$. Among all measurable functions $f$ with $\mathbb{E}\|f(Y)\|^2 < \infty$,
$$
\arg\min_f \; \mathbb{E}\, \|X - f(Y)\|^2 = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y].
$$

::: proof
Write
$$
X - f(Y) = (X - \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]) + (\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] - f(Y)).
$$
The second term is a function of $Y$, and the first is orthogonal to every square-integrable function of $Y$ by the defining property of conditional expectation. The cross term therefore vanishes, and
$$
\mathbb{E}\|X - f(Y)\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\|X - \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] - f(Y)\|^2 ,
$$
which is minimal exactly when $f(Y) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]$ almost surely. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — Why MSE networks blur]{.tag} Suppose that, given a coarse log, a sharp boundary between values 0 and 1 is equally likely at fine positions $p$ and $p + 1$.

-   The posterior mean is 0 before $p$, 0.5 between $p$ and $p + 1$, and 1 after.
-   That two-step ramp is a blurred edge that no real log contains.

A network trained with squared error converges towards this average (Theorem 3.3), hence the familiar smooth look of MSE super-resolution.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — The absolute loss gives the median]{.tag} For a real random variable $X$ with a continuous distribution,
$$
\arg\min_{c \in \mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E}\, |X - c| = \operatorname{med}(X).
$$
Trained per sample with the absolute loss, a network estimates the conditional median.

::: proof
The function $\varphi(c) = \mathbb{E}|X - c|$ is convex with derivative $\varphi'(c) = \mathbb{P}(X < c) - \mathbb{P}(X > c)$. It vanishes exactly where half of the mass lies on each side. [∎]{.qed}
:::

In Example 3.4 any value in $[0, 1]$ is a median at the ambiguous sample, so the absolute loss allows a sharp edge, although it does not choose where. The L1 loss is the default of many super-resolution networks for this reason.
::::

Blau and Michaeli (2018) proved a **perception–distortion trade-off**: at a given level of realism, measured as a divergence between the distribution of outputs and that of real signals, the lowest achievable distortion increases as realism is pushed further. Adversarial networks such as SRGAN (Ledig et al., 2017) gain realism by giving up PSNR.

In geoscience, realism without fidelity is dangerous: a sharp but invented fracture is worse than a blurred real one. Two safeguards follow. First, check **data consistency**: the residual $\|A\hat x - y\|$ should match the noise level. Second, prefer methods that report uncertainty, such as posterior sampling (ch. 10).

### 3.4 Deep super-resolution networks

-   **SRCNN** (Dong et al., 2016) upsamples by bicubic interpolation, then applies three convolutional layers read as patch extraction, nonlinear mapping and reconstruction.
-   **Residual learning** (VDSR, Kim, Lee and Lee, 2016) predicts the difference between the fine signal and the interpolated input, which is mostly high-frequency and easier to learn with a deep network.
-   **Sub-pixel convolution** (Shi et al., 2016) computes in the coarse grid and rearranges $s^2$ channels into an image $s$ times larger, which is cheaper.

The training pairs are the weak point. Real high-resolution geology is rarely observed, so pairs are usually synthesised by applying a model of the tool response to high-resolution data. The network then learns that model, not the real tool, and the gap between them is a distribution shift (ch. 9.2). When two tools of different resolution log the same interval, their depth-aligned data (ch. 5) give real pairs.

::: ex
[Example 3.6 — Four-fold super-resolution of a blocky log]{.tag} Code 3.7 degrades piecewise-constant logs by an 8-sample box blur, decimation by 4 and noise of standard deviation 0.05, then compares three estimators on a test log (root mean squared error, RMSE).

-   Linear interpolation: 0.408.
-   Tikhonov with a first-difference penalty: 0.349.
-   A three-layer 1D CNN trained with the absolute loss on 32 synthetic logs: 0.323.

The gains are modest, as Proposition 3.2 predicts: three quarters of the fine signal lies in directions the data do not see, and only the learned prior of blocky layers recovers part of it, near bed boundaries.
:::

**Code 3.7 — super-resolution of a synthetic log (about 10 s on a laptop CPU).**

```python
import numpy as np, torch
from scipy.sparse import diags, csr_matrix
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
torch.manual_seed(0)
torch.set_num_threads(1)
N, s, width, sigma = 512, 4, 8, 0.05      # fine samples, factor, tool width, noise

def blocky_log():                          # piecewise-constant "true" log
    edges = np.cumsum(rng.geometric(1 / 12, size=N))
    vals = rng.standard_normal(len(edges) + 1)
    return vals[np.searchsorted(edges, np.arange(N), side="right")]

A = np.zeros((N // s, N))                  # decimation o box blur (Def. 3.1)
for i in range(N // s):
    c = i * s + s // 2
    A[i, max(0, c - width // 2):c + width // 2] = 1 / width
def measure(x):
    return A @ x + sigma * rng.standard_normal(N // s)

train = [blocky_log() for _ in range(32)]
x_true = blocky_log()
y = measure(x_true)
rmse = lambda u: np.sqrt(np.mean((u - x_true) ** 2))

# (a) linear interpolation of the coarse samples
centres = np.arange(N // s) * s + s // 2
print("linear interpolation:", round(rmse(np.interp(np.arange(N), centres, y)), 3))

# (b) Tikhonov with a first-difference penalty (closed form, see ch. 8)
As = csr_matrix(A)
D = diags([-1.0, 1.0], [0, 1], shape=(N - 1, N))
x_tik = spsolve((As.T @ As + 0.02 * D.T @ D).tocsc(), As.T @ y)
print("Tikhonov            :", round(rmse(x_tik), 3))

# (c) a small 1D CNN trained on synthetic pairs (x, A x + noise)
net = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Upsample(scale_factor=s, mode="linear"),
    torch.nn.Conv1d(1, 16, 9, padding=4), torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Conv1d(16, 16, 9, padding=4), torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Conv1d(16, 1, 9, padding=4))
X = torch.tensor(np.stack(train), dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
for it in range(400):
    Y = torch.tensor(np.stack([measure(x) for x in train]), dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]
    loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(net(Y) - X))          # L1 loss (Prop. 3.5)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
with torch.no_grad():
    x_cnn = net(torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32)[None, None])[0, 0].numpy()
print("1D CNN (L1 loss)    :", round(rmse(x_cnn), 3))
```

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::

-   Super-resolution inverts blur plus decimation; the kernel of the operator has dimension at least $N(1 - 1/s)$.
-   Only a prior selects a solution: smoothness, sparsity, or a prior learned from examples.
-   Squared error yields the posterior mean, hence blur; absolute error yields the median and allows sharp edges.
-   Realism and fidelity trade off; in geoscience, check data consistency before trusting a sharp output.
-   Deep networks (SRCNN, residual, sub-pixel) are only as good as the tool model that generated their training pairs.
::::

## 4. Quality measures and ranking {#ch4}

Every later decision rests on comparisons: is this reconstruction better than that one, is this interval of log reliable, which of ten models should be deployed? This chapter defines measures of quality, with and without a reference, and the tools that turn comparisons into rankings.

### 4.1 Full-reference measures

MSE and PSNR (Definition 2.1) compare a reconstruction with a reference pixel by pixel. They ignore where the error is and what it looks like, which motivated the structural similarity index.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Structural similarity (SSIM)]{.tag} On a window of two images $a$ and $b$, with local means $\mu_a, \mu_b$, variances $\sigma_a^2, \sigma_b^2$ and covariance $\sigma_{ab}$:
$$
\mathrm{SSIM}(a, b) = \frac{2\mu_a\mu_b + C_1}{\mu_a^2 + \mu_b^2 + C_1} \cdot \frac{2\sigma_{ab} + C_2}{\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_b^2 + C_2},
$$
with small constants $C_1, C_2 > 0$. The first factor compares luminance, the second contrast and structure; the index of an image is the average over sliding windows (Wang et al., 2004).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — SSIM is at most 1]{.tag} On every window, for non-negative images,
$$
\mathrm{SSIM}(a, b) \le 1,
$$
with equality if and only if $a = b$ on the window.

::: proof
1.  $2\mu_a\mu_b \le \mu_a^2 + \mu_b^2$, so the first factor lies in $(0, 1]$, with equality if and only if $\mu_a = \mu_b$.
2.  By Cauchy–Schwarz, $\sigma_{ab} \le \sigma_a \sigma_b$, and $2\sigma_a\sigma_b \le \sigma_a^2 + \sigma_b^2$. The second factor is therefore at most 1, with equality if and only if $\sigma_a = \sigma_b$ and the correlation is 1.
3.  The product is at most 1, with equality only when both factors equal 1: equal means, equal variances and correlation 1, that is $a - \mu_a = b - \mu_b$ and thus $a = b$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — Same PSNR, different damage]{.tag} Code 4.8 degrades a striped test image in three ways, each scaled to an MSE of 0.01 (PSNR = 20 dB).

| Degradation | PSNR | SSIM |
|---|---|---|
| uniform brightness offset | 20.00 dB | 0.964 |
| white noise | 20.00 dB | 0.900 |
| Gaussian blur | 20.00 dB | 0.904 |

PSNR cannot tell them apart; SSIM penalises the loss of structure more than a harmless offset.
:::

The best quality measure is the one tied to the decision. For a super-resolved image, it may be the error on dips picked from it (Theorem 1.5); for an enhanced log, the facies accuracy downstream (ch. 7); for an inversion, the error on impedance at a blind well (ch. 8). Optimising a proxy too hard can degrade the task it stands for.

### 4.2 Quality without a reference

In the field there is no ground truth, yet each log and image must be checked before use. Quality control relies on indicators computed from the data alone.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.4 — Robust estimation of the noise level]{.tag} Let $d_1, \dots, d_m$ be fine-scale coefficients that are pure Gaussian noise $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, except for a small fraction affected by the signal. The estimator
$$
\hat \sigma = \frac{\operatorname{med}(|d_1|, \dots, |d_m|)}{0.6745}
$$
is consistent when that fraction tends to zero (Donoho and Johnstone, 1994).

::: proof
For $d \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, $\mathbb{P}(|d| \le c) = 2\Phi(c/\sigma) - 1$, which equals $\frac12$ for $c = \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}(3/4) = 0.6745\, \sigma$. The empirical median converges to that population median, and a vanishing fraction of outliers moves the median by a vanishing amount. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a log, the fine-scale coefficients can simply be first differences divided by $\sqrt 2$. Other no-reference indicators include the coverage fraction of an image, the fraction of saturated values, a sharpness score such as gradient energy, the agreement between redundant sensors, and physical plausibility (a density outside the range of minerals flags a bad interval).

Experts can also grade quality directly. Absolute grades are noisy and drift between experts, whereas a preference between two candidates is easier to give and more consistent. This turns quality assessment into a ranking problem.

### 4.3 Ranking

::: def
[Definition 4.5 — Ranking metrics]{.tag} For two rankings of $n$ items, a pair is concordant when both rankings order it the same way. **Kendall's tau** is
$$
\tau = \frac{\#\text{concordant} - \#\text{discordant}}{\binom{n}{2}} \in [-1, 1].
$$
For a ranked list with graded relevances $\mathrm{rel}_i$, the **discounted cumulative gain** is
$$
\mathrm{DCG}@k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{2^{\mathrm{rel}_i} - 1}{\log_2(i + 1)},
$$
and NDCG divides it by the DCG of the ideal order (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002).
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.6 — Does the metric agree with the experts?]{.tag} Six reconstruction methods have PSNR 31.2, 29.8, 30.5, 27.9, 28.4 and 32.0 dB; experts rank them 2, 4, 1, 6, 5, 3.

-   The metric puts method 6 first, then 1 and 3; the experts put 3, then 1 and 6.
-   The pairs (6, 1), (6, 3) and (1, 3) are discordant; the other 12 of the 15 pairs agree.
-   Hence $\tau = (12 - 3)/15 = 0.6$.

For a search engine that returns intervals with relevances (3, 2, 3, 0, 1), $\mathrm{DCG}@5 = 12.78$ and the ideal order (3, 3, 2, 1, 0) gives 13.35, so NDCG = 0.957.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.7 — Bradley–Terry scores are a convex problem]{.tag} Model the probability that item $i$ is preferred to item $j$ as
$$
\mathbb{P}(i \succ j) = \sigma(s_i - s_j), \qquad \sigma(u) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-u}}
$$
(Bradley and Terry, 1952). The negative log-likelihood of observed preferences is convex in $s \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and invariant under $s \mapsto s + c\mathbf{1}$. If the graph of compared pairs is connected, it is strictly convex on the hyperplane $s_1 = 0$.

::: proof
1.  Each observation "$i$ beats $j$" contributes $\ell(s_i - s_j)$ with $\ell(u) = -\log \sigma(u)$. Since $\ell''(u) = \sigma(u)(1 - \sigma(u)) > 0$, each term is a convex function of a linear form, and so is the sum.
2.  The Hessian is a weighted graph Laplacian on the compared pairs:
    $$
    \nabla^2 = \sum_{\text{obs}} \ell''(s_i - s_j)\,(e_i - e_j)(e_i - e_j)^\top .
    $$
3.  Its kernel is spanned by the constant vectors exactly when the comparison graph is connected, so it is positive definite on $\{s_1 = 0\}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Strict convexity gives uniqueness, but a minimiser exists only if no group of items wins all its comparisons against the rest; otherwise their scores run to infinity (Ford, 1957).
::::

RankNet (Burges et al., 2005) replaces free scores by a network $s_i = f_\theta(x_i)$ computed from the image or log $x_i$, trained with the same pairwise loss. The network then generalises: it scores new data with the preferences learned from experts.

**Code 4.8 — SSIM, Kendall's tau and Bradley–Terry scores.**

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import uniform_filter, gaussian_filter
from scipy.stats import kendalltau
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
j = np.arange(128)
x = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (j[:, None] + 8 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * j[None, :] / 128)) / 16)
x = (x + 1) / 2                                    # reference image in [0, 1]

def ssim(a, b, L=1.0, win=7):                      # Definition 4.1, local windows
    C1, C2 = (0.01 * L) ** 2, (0.03 * L) ** 2
    mu_a, mu_b = uniform_filter(a, win), uniform_filter(b, win)
    va = uniform_filter(a * a, win) - mu_a ** 2
    vb = uniform_filter(b * b, win) - mu_b ** 2
    cov = uniform_filter(a * b, win) - mu_a * mu_b
    m = ((2 * mu_a * mu_b + C1) * (2 * cov + C2)) / ((mu_a**2 + mu_b**2 + C1) * (va + vb + C2))
    return m.mean()

psnr = lambda a, b: 10 * np.log10(1 / np.mean((a - b) ** 2))
target_mse = 0.01                                  # three degradations, same MSE
shift = x + np.sqrt(target_mse)                    # brightness offset
noise = rng.standard_normal(x.shape)
noisy = x + noise * np.sqrt(target_mse / np.mean(noise ** 2))
blur = gaussian_filter(x, 1.0)
blur = x + (blur - x) * np.sqrt(target_mse / np.mean((blur - x) ** 2))
for name, im in [("offset", shift), ("noise", noisy), ("blur", blur)]:
    print(f"{name:6s}  PSNR = {psnr(x, im):5.2f} dB   SSIM = {ssim(x, im):.3f}")

# Kendall tau between a metric ranking and an expert ranking of 6 methods
metric_scores = [31.2, 29.8, 30.5, 27.9, 28.4, 32.0]
expert_rank = [2, 4, 1, 6, 5, 3]                   # 1 = best
tau, _ = kendalltau(metric_scores, [-r for r in expert_rank])
print(f"Kendall tau(metric, expert) = {tau:.3f}")

# Bradley-Terry scores from pairwise expert votes (Theorem 4.7)
true_s = np.array([0.0, 0.8, 1.5, -0.5])
pairs, wins = [], []
for _ in range(400):
    i, k = rng.choice(4, 2, replace=False)
    d = np.zeros(4); d[i], d[k] = 1, -1
    pairs.append(d)
    wins.append(rng.random() < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(true_s[i] - true_s[k]))))
bt = LogisticRegression(fit_intercept=False, C=10.0).fit(np.array(pairs), wins)
s_hat = bt.coef_[0] - bt.coef_[0][0]               # fix the gauge s_0 = 0
print("Bradley-Terry scores:", s_hat.round(2), " true:", true_s)
```

With 400 simulated votes on four items, the fitted scores are (0, 0.78, 1.56, −0.37) against (0, 0.8, 1.5, −0.5) in truth: logistic regression on difference vectors is exactly Bradley–Terry maximum likelihood, with a mild $\ell_2$ penalty.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::

-   PSNR measures energy of the error; SSIM compares local means, contrasts and correlations, and equals 1 only for identical images.
-   The right quality measure is the one tied to the decision the data will support.
-   Without a reference, robust statistics (the median absolute deviation) and physical checks estimate quality.
-   Kendall's tau compares rankings, NDCG scores ranked lists with graded relevance.
-   Pairwise preferences give scores through the convex Bradley–Terry likelihood; RankNet learns them from the data.
::::

## 5. Data alignment {#ch5}

Two logging runs in the same well rarely agree in depth: the cable stretches, the tool sticks and slips, and depth references differ. Cores carry their own depths, and seismic lives in time rather than depth. Alignment comes before any learning on several sources, because a misaligned label is a wrong label.

### 5.1 Constant shifts: cross-correlation and phase correlation

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.1 — Least squares and correlation select the same shift]{.tag} Let $S_\tau$ be the circular shift by $\tau$ samples. For signals $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
$$
\arg\min_\tau \|x - S_\tau y\|^2 = \arg\max_\tau \langle x, S_\tau y \rangle .
$$

::: proof
Expand the square:
$$
\|x - S_\tau y\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + \|S_\tau y\|^2 - 2\langle x, S_\tau y\rangle .
$$
A shift permutes the samples, so $\|S_\tau y\| = \|y\|$, and only the last term depends on $\tau$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

All $n$ correlations are computed at once with the FFT, in $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$, since a correlation is a convolution with a reversed signal (Proposition 0.4). For non-circular logs, the overlap changes with $\tau$, so the correlation is computed on a common interior window or normalised.
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Phase correlation]{.tag} If $y = S_\tau x$, then $\hat y_\ell = e^{-2i\pi \ell\tau/n}\, \hat x_\ell$. If $\hat x_\ell \neq 0$ for every $\ell$, the normalised cross-power spectrum is a pure phase, and its inverse DFT is a spike at $\tau$:
$$
\mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\left[\frac{\hat y_\ell\, \overline{\hat x_\ell}}{|\hat y_\ell\, \overline{\hat x_\ell}|}\right] = \delta_\tau .
$$

::: proof
The shift theorem follows from Definition 0.3 by the change of index $k \mapsto k - \tau$. The ratio then equals $e^{-2i\pi\ell\tau/n}$ for every $\ell$, and the inverse DFT of this sequence is the Kronecker delta at $\tau$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Phase correlation ignores gains and slow trends, extends to 2D translations of images, and handles rotation and scaling after a log-polar resampling. On a borehole image, a rotation of the tool around its axis is a circular shift in azimuth, so it is estimated this way.

### 5.2 Non-linear alignment: dynamic time warping

When the shift varies with depth, a single lag is not enough.

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Warping path]{.tag} For two sequences $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ and $b = (b_1, \dots, b_m)$, a **warping path** is a sequence of index pairs $(i_k, j_k)$.

It starts at $(1, 1)$, ends at $(n, m)$, and at each step advances in one sequence or in both.

Its cost, for a local distance $d$ such as the squared difference, is
$$
\sum_k d(a_{i_k}, b_{j_k}).
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.4 — Dynamic programming computes the optimal warping]{.tag} Set $C(0, 0) = 0$ and $C(i, 0) = C(0, j) = +\infty$ otherwise, and
$$
C(i, j) = d(a_i, b_j) + \min\{C(i-1, j-1),\; C(i-1, j),\; C(i, j-1)\}.
$$
Then $C(n, m)$ is the minimal cost over all warping paths, computed in $\mathcal{O}(nm)$ operations; a band $|i - j| \le w$ reduces this to $\mathcal{O}(nw)$ (Sakoe and Chiba, 1978).

::: proof
By induction on $i + j$, $C(i, j)$ is the minimal cost of a path from $(1, 1)$ to $(i, j)$. An optimal path to $(i, j)$ arrives from one of its three predecessors. Its prefix is then a path to that predecessor, and it must be optimal: otherwise replacing it by a cheaper one would lower the total. The minimum over the three predecessors is therefore the optimal cost. Backtracking the minimising choices recovers the path. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.5 — A warping by hand]{.tag} Align $a = (0, 2, 1)$ with $b = (0, 1, 2, 1)$ using the squared difference. The table $C(i, j)$ is
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 5 & 6 \\ 4 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 5 & 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix},
$$
so the optimal cost is 1. One optimal path matches $0 \leftrightarrow 0$, $0 \leftrightarrow 1$, $2 \leftrightarrow 2$, $1 \leftrightarrow 1$. The value 1 in $b$ has no counterpart in $a$, so one unit of cost is unavoidable.
:::

The constraints carry geology. Monotone steps preserve the stratigraphic order (layers cannot swap), the band encodes the largest plausible depth error, and slope limits forbid absurd stretching. Soft-DTW (Cuturi and Blondel, 2017) replaces the minimum by a smooth minimum, which makes the alignment cost differentiable and usable as a training loss.

### 5.3 Rigid registration

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.6 — Orthogonal Procrustes (Kabsch)]{.tag} Let $p_i, q_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be paired points with zero centroids, and let $H = \sum_i p_i q_i^\top = U \Sigma V^\top$ (SVD). Over rotations $R \in SO(d)$, the sum $\sum_i \|R p_i - q_i\|^2$ is minimised by
$$
R^\star = V \operatorname{diag}(1, \dots, 1, \det(V U^\top))\, U^\top .
$$

::: proof
1.  Expanding, and using $\sum_i q_i^\top R p_i = \operatorname{tr}(R H)$:
    $$
    \sum_i \|Rp_i - q_i\|^2 = \sum_i (\|p_i\|^2 + \|q_i\|^2) - 2\operatorname{tr}(R H).
    $$
2.  With $M = V^\top R U$, which is orthogonal, so that $M_{kk} \le 1$:
    $$
    \operatorname{tr}(RH) = \operatorname{tr}(V^\top R U \Sigma) = \sum_k M_{kk}\sigma_k \le \sum_k \sigma_k .
    $$
3.  Equality holds for $M = I$, that is $R = VU^\top$, which is a rotation when $\det(VU^\top) = 1$.
4.  Otherwise $\det M = -1$ is imposed, and the best choice flips the sign attached to the smallest $\sigma_d$, which gives the stated formula (Kabsch, 1976). [∎]{.qed}
:::

With non-centred data, first translate both sets to their centroids; the optimal translation then maps one centroid onto the other.
::::

Rigid registration aligns repeated passes of a tool, matches 3D surveys, and registers images from different tools once a few common features are identified. Learned registration replaces hand-picked features by networks: spatial transformer networks (Jaderberg et al., 2015) predict a transformation inside a network, and VoxelMorph (Balakrishnan et al., 2019) learns deformable registration fields from pairs of images.

### 5.4 The well-to-seismic tie

The tie aligns a well, measured in depth, with seismic, measured in time. It chains the tools of ch. 1 and of this chapter.

1.  Compute the impedance log $Z = \rho v$ from the density and sonic logs.
2.  Convert depth to two-way time with the sonic velocities, $t(z) = 2\int_0^z dz'/v(z')$, corrected by check-shot measurements when they exist.
3.  Compute the reflectivity (Definition 1.7) and convolve it with a wavelet to get a synthetic trace.
4.  Match the synthetic and the real trace: a bulk shift by cross-correlation (5.1), then a gentle stretch-and-squeeze with a narrow-band DTW (5.2), while estimating the wavelet.

The tie produces the time–depth relation that transfers well labels (facies, impedance) onto the seismic, and the low-frequency model that inversion needs (ch. 8.4).

::: ex
[Example 5.7 — Depth matching two logging runs]{.tag} Code 5.8 simulates two gamma-ray runs whose depth offset varies smoothly from 5 to 20 samples.

-   The best constant lag, found by cross-correlation, is 16 samples; it leaves a mean depth error of 2.43 samples in the interior.
-   Banded DTW follows the varying offset and reduces the mean error to 0.76 samples.
:::

**Code 5.8 — constant shift versus dynamic time warping.**

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter1d

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
gr = gaussian_filter1d(rng.standard_normal(n + 80), 3)       # "true" gamma-ray log
ref = gr[40:40 + n] + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n)          # reference run

# second run: depth shift of 5 samples plus a slow stretch (cable effects)
u = np.arange(n)
warp = u + 5 + 15 * np.sin(np.pi * u / n)                     # true depth map
run2 = np.interp(warp + 40, np.arange(n + 80), gr) + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n)

# (1) constant shift by cross-correlation (Proposition 5.1)
lags = np.arange(-30, 31)
cc = [np.dot(ref[40:-40], run2[40 + l:n - 40 + l]) for l in lags]
best = lags[int(np.argmax(cc))]
print("cross-correlation lag:", best, "samples")

# (2) dynamic time warping with a Sakoe-Chiba band (Theorem 5.4)
def dtw(a, b, band=25):
    na, nb = len(a), len(b)
    C = np.full((na + 1, nb + 1), np.inf)
    C[0, 0] = 0.0
    for i in range(1, na + 1):
        for j in range(max(1, i - band), min(nb, i + band) + 1):
            d = (a[i - 1] - b[j - 1]) ** 2
            C[i, j] = d + min(C[i - 1, j - 1], C[i - 1, j], C[i, j - 1])
    i, j, path = na, nb, []                                  # backtracking
    while i > 0 and j > 0:
        path.append((i - 1, j - 1))
        k = np.argmin([C[i - 1, j - 1], C[i - 1, j], C[i, j - 1]])
        i, j = (i - 1, j - 1) if k == 0 else ((i - 1, j) if k == 1 else (i, j - 1))
    return C[na, nb], path[::-1]

cost, path = dtw(ref, run2)
# ref sample i matches run2 sample j  <=>  i = warp[j]; compare in the interior
est = {}
for i, j in path:
    est.setdefault(j, []).append(i)
js = np.array([j for j in est if 60 < j < n - 60])
err_dtw = np.mean([abs(np.mean(est[j]) - warp[j]) for j in js])
err_cc = np.mean(np.abs((js - best) - warp[js]))   # run2[j] ~ ref[j - lag]
print(f"mean depth error: constant shift {err_cc:.2f}, DTW {err_dtw:.2f} samples")
```

The printed lag is −16 in the code's convention (sample $j$ of the second run matches sample $j + 16$ of the reference).

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::

-   For a constant shift, least squares and cross-correlation agree, and the FFT computes all lags at once.
-   Phase correlation turns a translation into a spike and ignores gains and trends.
-   Dynamic time warping finds the optimal monotone alignment by dynamic programming; bands and slopes encode geological limits.
-   The best rotation between paired point sets comes from an SVD (Procrustes, Kabsch).
-   The well-to-seismic tie chains impedance, time conversion, synthetic traces and alignment.
::::

## 6. Contrast enhancement and inpainting {#ch6}

Raw images are often hard to read: a few extreme values crush the contrast, and parts of the wall are not measured at all. This chapter treats both problems: remapping values so that structure becomes visible, and filling gaps with values consistent with their surroundings.

### 6.1 Contrast enhancement

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Point transform]{.tag} A point transform replaces every value $u$ of an image by $T(u)$ for a non-decreasing function $T$. Examples are windowing (clip to $[u_{\min}, u_{\max}]$ and rescale), the logarithm (natural for resistivity, ch. 1.2) and the gamma correction $T(u) = u^\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Histogram equalisation]{.tag} Let $U$ be a real random variable with a continuous distribution function $F$. Then
$$
F(U) \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1).
$$

::: proof
Let $F^{-}(t) = \inf\{u : F(u) \ge t\}$ for $t \in (0, 1)$. By continuity of $F$, $F(F^{-}(t)) = t$.

Moreover $F(U) \le t$ holds exactly when $U \le F^{-}(t)$, up to an event of probability zero. Hence
$$
\mathbb{P}(F(U) \le t) = F(F^{-}(t)) = t. \qquad
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

On an image, $F$ is the empirical distribution function, and the equalised value of a pixel is its rank divided by the number of pixels.
::::

Borehole images are distributed in two renderings. **Static normalisation** uses one mapping for the whole well, which keeps values comparable between depths and shows large-scale changes. **Dynamic normalisation** recomputes the mapping in a sliding depth window, which reveals fractures and fine bedding everywhere but destroys absolute levels. Interpreters need both, for different questions.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — Equalisation amplifies where the histogram peaks]{.tag} If $U$ has density $p$, the equalising map $T = F$ has slope $T'(u) = p(u)$. A small perturbation $\delta$ of a value $u$ becomes, after equalisation,
$$
T(u + \delta) - T(u) \approx p(u)\, \delta .
$$
Clipping the density at a level $c$ and renormalising it before integrating bounds the slope, hence the amplification, by $c / \kappa$, where $\kappa \le 1$ is the mass that survives the clipping.

::: proof
$F$ is differentiable with $F' = p$, and the first-order Taylor expansion gives the approximation. The clipped density $\min(p, c)$ has mass $\kappa$, so the new map has density $\min(p, c)/\kappa$, and its slope is at most $c/\kappa$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Flat, noisy regions have a peaked histogram, so plain equalisation turns their noise into strong texture. **CLAHE** (Zuiderveld, 1994) clips the histogram, redistributes the excess, computes the map in tiles, and blends neighbouring tiles bilinearly. Learned enhancement networks can mimic the renderings interpreters prefer, at the risk of learning the taste of a single expert (ch. 9.1).

### 6.2 Inpainting

::: def
[Definition 6.4 — Inpainting]{.tag} An image $f$ is known on a domain $\Omega$ except on a set $D$ (the mask). Inpainting computes values on $D$ that are consistent with $f$ on $\Omega \setminus D$. Typical masks are the vertical gaps between the pads of a resistivity imager, dead seismic traces, and log intervals lost in washed-out borehole sections.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.5 — Harmonic inpainting]{.tag} On a pixel grid, let $E(u) = \sum_{p \sim q} (u_p - u_q)^2$ over pairs of neighbouring pixels, with $u = f$ fixed outside $D$. If every connected component of $D$ has a neighbour outside $D$, then $E$ has a unique minimiser. In it, every unknown pixel is the average of its neighbours (a discrete harmonic function), and its values stay between the minimum and the maximum of the known values.

::: proof
1.  $E$ is a quadratic function of the unknowns $u_D$. Setting its partial derivative at $p \in D$ to zero gives $u_p = \frac{1}{\deg p}\sum_{q \sim p} u_q$.
2.  The quadratic part is $u_D^\top L_{DD}\, u_D$, where $L_{DD}$ is the graph Laplacian restricted to $D$. It equals the sum of $(u_p - u_q)^2$ over edges inside the mask, plus $u_p^2$ over edges leaving it.
3.  If this sum vanishes, $u$ is constant on each component of $D$ and zero next to its boundary, hence zero. So $L_{DD}$ is positive definite and the minimiser is unique.
4.  At a maximum of $u$ inside $D$, the average of the neighbours equals the maximum, so all neighbours share it. Walking to the boundary shows that it is reached on known pixels; the minimum is similar. [∎]{.qed}
:::

In the continuous limit, the minimiser of $\int_D |\nabla u|^2$ with boundary data $f$ solves the Laplace equation $\Delta u = 0$ in $D$.
::::

::: ex
[Example 6.6 — Filling pad gaps]{.tag} Code 6.7 builds an equalised image of dipping beds and removes 25 % of the azimuths in four vertical gaps, as a four-pad tool would.

-   Filling each gap with the mean of the known pixels leaves an RMSE of 0.290 in the gaps.
-   Harmonic inpainting, periodic in azimuth, reduces it to 0.139.
-   The equalised image has exactly flat histogram bins (2457 or 2458 pixels in each fifth).
:::

Harmonic filling is smooth, so it cannot continue thin sinusoids across wide gaps: it averages them away. Other models keep more structure:

-   **Total variation** inpainting (Shen and Chan, 2002) minimises $\int_D |\nabla u|$ and preserves edges, although it joins them by straight segments.
-   **Exemplar-based** methods (Criminisi, Pérez and Toyama, 2004) copy patches from the known region along the isophotes.
-   **Multiple-point statistics** fill borehole images with patterns learned from the measured part (Hurley and Zhang, 2011).
-   **Geometric models** fit the sinusoids of Theorem 1.5 on the visible pieces and extend them across the gaps: physics as a prior.

Deep inpainting has two families. **Partial convolutions** (Liu et al., 2018) renormalise each convolution over the valid pixels of its window and update the mask from layer to layer; they are trained on large image collections with random masks. **Deep Image Prior** (Ulyanov, Vedaldi and Lempitsky, 2018) needs no training data. It fits a randomly initialised network $g_\theta(z)$ to the known pixels only,
$$
\min_\theta \|M \odot (g_\theta(z) - f)\|^2 ,
$$
where $M$ is the indicator of known pixels, and stops early. The architecture itself acts as the prior.

To measure inpainting error honestly, hide known pixels with an artificial mask shaped like the real gaps and compare. No other measurement is possible, since the true values in the gaps are never observed.

**Code 6.7 — histogram equalisation and harmonic inpainting.**

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import lil_matrix
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
H, W = 96, 128
z, j = np.mgrid[0:H, 0:W].astype(float)
phi = 2 * np.pi * j / W
img = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (z + 10 * np.cos(phi - 1.0)) / 20)       # dipping beds
img = np.exp(1.5 * img) + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal((H, W))     # skewed values

# histogram equalisation (Theorem 6.2): map each value through the empirical CDF
ranks = np.argsort(np.argsort(img.ravel()))
eq = ((ranks + 0.5) / img.size).reshape(H, W)
print("histogram of equalised image (5 bins):", np.histogram(eq, 5, (0, 1))[0])

# pad tool: 4 pads, each covering 75% of its quarter of the circumference
mask = (j % 32) < 24                                              # True = measured
known = np.where(mask, eq, 0.0)

# harmonic inpainting (Theorem 6.5): discrete Laplace equation in the gaps,
# periodic in azimuth, known pixels as Dirichlet data
idx = -np.ones((H, W), dtype=int)
idx[~mask] = np.arange((~mask).sum())
M = lil_matrix(((~mask).sum(),) * 2)
b = np.zeros((~mask).sum())
for (r, c) in zip(*np.nonzero(~mask)):
    k = idx[r, c]
    nbrs = [(r, (c - 1) % W), (r, (c + 1) % W)] + [(rr, c) for rr in (r - 1, r + 1) if 0 <= rr < H]
    M[k, k] = len(nbrs)
    for rr, cc in nbrs:
        if mask[rr, cc]:
            b[k] += known[rr, cc]
        else:
            M[k, idx[rr, cc]] -= 1
filled = known.copy()
filled[~mask] = spsolve(M.tocsr(), b)
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((filled[~mask] - eq[~mask]) ** 2))
print(f"gap fraction {1 - mask.mean():.0%}, harmonic RMSE in the gaps = {rmse:.3f}")
print(f"RMSE of a constant fill with the mean = {np.sqrt(np.mean((eq[~mask] - eq[mask].mean()) ** 2)):.3f}")
```

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 6
:::

-   Point transforms remap values; equalisation through the distribution function makes the histogram uniform.
-   Static normalisation keeps values comparable along the well, dynamic normalisation reveals local detail.
-   Equalisation amplifies noise where the histogram peaks; CLAHE bounds that gain by clipping.
-   Harmonic inpainting solves a discrete Laplace equation, with a unique solution and no overshoot.
-   Edge-preserving, exemplar, geometric and deep methods keep more structure; measure them with artificial masks.
::::

## 7. Classification and segmentation {#ch7}

Interpretation assigns classes: a facies to each depth of a well, a label to each pixel of an image. This chapter covers both tasks, with one theme throughout: the validation must imitate the deployment, or the scores will lie.

### 7.1 Facies classification from logs

A facies is a body of rock with distinctive characteristics (lithology, texture, depositional environment). The task is to predict a facies $y_k \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ at each depth from the logs $x(z_k)$, using a few wells where geologists have labelled facies from cores and logs.

-   **Features**: the logs, their depth derivatives, and windows of neighbouring samples that give context.
-   **Models**, in order of complexity: logistic regression, random forests, gradient boosting such as XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016), and 1D convolutional or recurrent networks along depth.
-   **Public benchmark**: the tutorial and contest of Hall (2016) released labelled wells for this task.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — The risk that matters]{.tag} Let wells be drawn from a population, $W \sim P_W$, and let samples within a well follow $P_{\cdot \mid W}$. The risk of a classifier $f$ on a **new** well is
$$
R_{\mathrm{new}}(f) = \mathbb{E}_{W}\, \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim P_{\cdot \mid W}}\, \mathbb{1}[f(x) \ne y].
$$
:::

Random $K$-fold cross-validation draws test samples from wells that also supply training samples, often from the next depth.
